3kieou:191: The original text explicitly states: "Core competition has begun shifting from model selection to engineering capability building." When AI systems scale, the following issues become fatal: how to control hallucinations, how to explain decisions, how to coordinate multiple systems, how to conduct evaluation, and how to implement security and compliance. These issues, treated as "side matters" in the PoC phase, become backbone issues that determine whether a project can continue in production. The lack of a complete engineering methodology leads to: every launch relies on experience, every expansion repeats the same pitfalls, the system is usable but unstable, and teams are busy but the reuse rate is extremely low.
4fmkkn:84: This is not an issue for individual teams; in 2026, enterprise AI deployment is collectively entering the same deep-water zone. What truly separates leaders today is no longer who connects to models first, but who first turns AI into a production system that runs sustainably.
5011n4:207: The original text points out: "What many enterprises truly lack is not more computing power, but the ability to get a return from existing computing power." This reveals a common phenomenon: enterprises often focus on procurement and deployment in AI investment, treating computing power as a static resource. However, production-grade AI systems need not more GPUs, but refined scheduling algorithms, low-level optimization, and chip adaptation capabilities. With the same hardware investment, different scheduling strategies can bring efficiency differences of several times. This cognitive misalignment leads enterprises to discover after completing the PoC: the model runs, but resource utilization stays low for a long time, and the cost structure cannot be optimized.
